{{Short description|Equation in geometry}}
In [[geometry]], the '''Cesàro equation''' of a [[plane curve]] is an [[equation]] relating the [[curvature]] ({{mvar|κ}}) at a point of the curve to the [[arc length]] ({{mvar|s}}) from the start of the curve to the given point. It may also be given as an equation relating the [[Radius of curvature (mathematics)|radius of curvature]] ({{mvar|R}}) to [[arc length]]. (These are equivalent because {{math|''R'' {{=}} {{sfrac|1|''κ''}}}}.) Two [[congruence (geometry)|congruent]] curves will have the same Cesàro equation. Cesàro equations are named after [[Ernesto Cesàro]].

==Log-aesthetic curves==

The family of log-aesthetic curves<ref>{{cite journal | author=Miura, K. T. | year=2006 | title=A General Equation of Aesthetic Curves and its Self-Affinity | journal=Computer-Aided Design and Applications | volume=3 | issue=1-4 | pages=457–464 | doi=10.1080/16864360.2006.10738484 }}</ref> is determined in the general (<math>\alpha \ne 0</math>) case by the following intrinsic equation:

<math>R(s)^\alpha = c_0s + c_1</math>

This is equivalent to the following explicit formula for curvature:

<math>\kappa(s) = (c_0s+c_1)^{-1/\alpha}</math>

Further, the <math>c_1</math> constant above represents simple re-parametrization of the arc length parameter, while <math>c_0</math> is equivalent to uniform scaling, so log-aesthetic curves are fully characterized by the <math>\alpha</math> parameter.

In the special case of <math>\alpha=0</math>, the log-aesthetic curve becomes [[Nielsen's spiral]], with the following Cesàro equation (where <math>a</math> is a uniform scaling parameter):

<math>\kappa(s) = \frac{e^{\frac{s}{a}}}{a}</math>

A number of well known curves are instances of the log-aesthetic curve family. These include circle (<math>\alpha = \infty</math>), [[Euler spiral]] (<math>\alpha = -1</math>), [[Logarithmic spiral]] (<math>\alpha = 1</math>), and [[Involute|Circle involute]] (<math>\alpha = 2</math>).

==Examples==
Some curves have a particularly simple representation by a Cesàro equation. Some examples are:
* [[line (geometry)|Line]]: <math>\kappa = 0</math>.
* [[Circle]]: <math>\kappa = \frac{1}{\alpha}</math>, where  <math>{\alpha}</math> is the radius.
* [[Logarithmic spiral]]: <math>\kappa=\frac{a}{s}</math>, where <math>{a}</math> is a constant.
* [[Involute|Circle involute]]: <math>\kappa=\frac{a}{\sqrt s}</math>, where <math>{a}</math> is a constant.
* [[Euler spiral]]: <math>\kappa=as</math>, where <math>{a}</math> is a constant.
* [[Catenary]]: <math>\kappa=\frac{a}{s^2+a^2}</math>, where <math>{a}</math> is a constant.

==Related parameterizations==
The Cesàro equation of a curve is related to its [[Whewell equation]] in the following way: if the Whewell equation is {{math|''φ'' {{=}} ''f''{{hairsp}}(''s'')}} then the Cesàro equation is {{math|''κ'' {{=}} ''f''{{prime}}(''s'')}}.
